extracted.intended_audience: general public, students and researchers interested in film industry history, film regulation, ratings, and anti‑piracy policy
extracted.subtask_description: Encyclopedic overview of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), its history, self‑regulation (Production Code), voluntary film rating system, anti‑piracy activities, and MPA awards; includes the specific content guidelines and procedural rules the organization has used. Useful for understanding film content standards and enforcement practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion Picture Production Code (Hays Code)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of moral guidelines introduced in 1930 that specified what was acceptable to include in films; incorporated many examples from earlier 'Don'ts and Be Carefuls'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Code prohibited, among other things, 'scenes of passion' unless essential to plot; 'pointed profanity' in word or action; 'sex perversion'; justification or explicit coverage of adultery; sympathetic treatment of crime or criminals; dancing with 'indecent' moves; and 'white slavery' (prostitution). The Code was the industry’s central self‑regulatory content standard until replaced by the voluntary rating system in 1968.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Don'ts and Be Carefuls" and 'The Formula'
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Formula" and the 'Don'ts and Be Carefuls' were early loose guidelines (1920s) the MPPDA used to advise studios on problematic content and local censorship risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Formula requested studios send synopses of films for review; the 'Don'ts and Be Carefuls' listed issues that could cause problems in different localities. These were advisory and largely ignored by studios (only ~20% of scripts were sent by 1929).

rubrics_metrics.name: Production Code Administration (PCA) binding enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: From 1934 the Production Code Administration made binding decisions: no film could be exhibited in an American theater without PCA approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PCA decisions were binding; films required a PCA stamp of approval to be exhibited, and producers attempting exhibition without approval faced fines (example cited: $25,000). The PCA returned films for edits or refused approval when standards were not met.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1956 Production Code revision (content limits and new restrictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1956 revision relaxed some prohibitions and tightened others: allowed treatment of certain subjects 'within the limits of good taste', and added restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowed treatment of subjects previously forbidden (e.g., abortion and narcotics) provided they were presented 'within the limits of good taste'; added new restrictions including outlawing depiction of blasphemy and mercy killings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replacement of the Production Code by a voluntary film rating system (1968)
rubrics_metrics.description: In 1968 the MPA (then MPAA) replaced the Production Code with a voluntary ratings system to limit censorship and provide parents with information about film appropriateness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rating system was intended to give parents guidance rather than to censor content; it is voluntary and carries no legal standing—industry participants enforce it through exhibition and distribution practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: CARA / Classification and Rating Administration — independence claim
rubrics_metrics.description: CARA (later Classification and Rating Administration) issues ratings and the MPA states ratings are made by an independent group of parents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MPA/CARA asserts that ratings are determined by an independent parental board; criticism has alleged lack of transparency and preferential treatment for member studios, which prompted the MPA to post ratings rules and an appeals process online.

rubrics_metrics.name: G — General Audiences rating meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: G – General Audiences: 'Nothing that would offend parents for viewing by children.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On packaging/box: 'All ages admitted'. Intended to signal material suitable for all ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: PG — Parental Guidance Suggested rating meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: PG – Parental Guidance Suggested: 'Parents urged to give 'parental guidance.' May contain some material parents might not like for their young children.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On packaging/box: 'Some material may not be suitable for children'.

rubrics_metrics.name: PG-13 — Parents Strongly Cautioned rating meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: PG-13 – Parents Strongly Cautioned: 'Parents are urged to be cautious. Some material may be inappropriate for pre‑teenagers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On packaging/box: 'Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13'.

rubrics_metrics.name: R — Restricted rating meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: R – Restricted: 'Contains some adult material. Parents are urged to learn more about the film before taking their young children with them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On packaging/box: 'Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian'. Industry policy commonly forbids admitting unaccompanied children to R‑rated films.

rubrics_metrics.name: NC-17 — Adults Only rating meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: NC-17 – Adults Only: 'Clearly adult. Children are not admitted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On packaging/box: 'No One 17 and Under Admitted'. Replaced the 'X' rating in 1990 to distinguish adult artistic work from pornography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratings system legal/industry status and exhibition practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The MPA ratings are voluntary and have no legal standing; the American film industry enforces them through theater and distributor policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many theaters refuse to exhibit non‑rated films; the industry enforces age‑related admission policies (e.g., unaccompanied children not admitted to R films). 'Unrated' films often denoted 'NR' in listings but that is not a formal MPA rating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratings transparency and appeals (post‑criticism disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: After criticism (e.g., This Film Is Not Yet Rated), the MPA posted its ratings rules, policies, procedures, and appeals process online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was presented as a response to allegations of preferential treatment and lack of transparency; the existence of a formal appeals process is part of the procedural rubric for handling disputes about ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright Alert System — identification, notice, mitigation and appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: A multi‑party system (MPAA, RIAA, ISPs) that used a third‑party service to identify allegedly infringing content and notify users; repeated notices could trigger mitigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Users received notices and information about authorized alternatives; multiple notices could lead to mitigation measures (e.g., temporary slowing of Internet service) but not to account termination; subscribers could appeal to the American Arbitration Association. The system was discontinued in January 2017.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPA anti‑piracy enforcement approaches and criteria for action
rubrics_metrics.description: The MPA has used a mix of educational campaigns, cease‑and‑desist letters, lawsuits against file‑sharing services and individuals, lobbying, and cooperation with foreign governments and law enforcement to combat piracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include sending thousands of letters to ISPs to forward to infringing users, filing suits against BitTorrent/eDonkey services and individuals, encouraging foreign raids (e.g., Pirate Bay), and supporting measures to treat electronic transmissions as 'articles' for import control. These methods reflect the organization's practical standards for identifying and responding to piracy threats.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPA Awards categories and their awarding criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of principal MPA Awards and the qualities each recognizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPA Creator Award: presented to an individual whose craft behind the camera has shaped culture and helped audiences see the world differently. MPA Industry Champion Award: given to individuals who promote growth of the creative economy by advancing dynamic policies that generate new opportunities for creators. MPA Creative Protector Award (new in 2024): honors an institution or individual demonstrating commitment to safeguarding creativity through effective anti‑piracy and enforcement actions. MPA Lifetime Achievement Award: recognizes those with unwavering commitment to the industry throughout their career.
